Benefit-year changes. Children’s birthdays during July 2026 to June 2027, shared custody, and changes in marital status change the CCB month by month.
Check which limit binds. If two-thirds of the lower earner’s earned income binds, extra paid care gives no deduction. If the per-child limits bind, it does not matter which child the care was for.
Collect receipts with the provider’s details. CRA requires a receipt for each payment; an individual provider’s receipt must show their social insurance number. Keep them if you file online.
File both returns on time. The CCB for July 2026 depends on both spouses having filed for 2025; a deduction claimed late is reassessed, and CRA recalculates the benefit.
Look at the other deductions. RRSP, FHSA and union dues also reduce family net income. A household inside a CCB reduction band gets the band’s rate on top of the tax saving from any of them.
Other income-tested amounts. The GST/HST credit, Canada workers benefit and child disability benefit also depend on family net income and can rise too.
Provincial programs. Ontario’s CARE credit and Quebec’s refundable child care credit, which replaces the deduction in Quebec for provincial tax, are not modelled, nor are provincial child benefits.

Special situations. Single parents, the higher-income spouse’s weekly claims, students, boarding schools and overnight camps, and children eligible for the disability tax credit are described but not modelled.
The exact tax. The tax saved is the deduction above the tax-free level times an editable rate. It ignores brackets the deduction may cross, other credits, and provincial reductions.
Use Form T778. Form T778 Parts A and B work out the deduction; Part C is only for a higher-income spouse in one of the listed situations, Part D for a claimant who was a student.
Years. Only the 2025 deduction and the July 2026 to June 2027 CCB amounts are used.

CRA’s CCB calculation for July 2026 to June 2027 uses 2025 adjusted family net income: the two spouses’ net incomes after deductions such as this one. The maximum is CAD 8,157 a year per child under 6 and CAD 6,883 per child aged 6 to 17. It is reduced as follows:

CRA’s page on who can claim is direct: the person with the lower net income, including zero income, must claim. If incomes are equal, the couple agree which of them claims. The higher-income spouse can claim only for the period in which the lower-income spouse was a student in a qualifying program, unable to care for children because of an infirmity or a hospital stay of two weeks or more (with a doctor’s statement), in prison for two weeks or more, or separated because of a breakdown in the relationship. Even then the claim is limited per week: the folio’s periodic amount is 1/40 of the annual amount, which works out to CAD 200, CAD 125 or CAD 275 a week per child.

For 2025, the child care expense deduction is the least of three amounts: eligible expenses paid, CAD 8,000 per child under 7 at year end plus CAD 5,000 per child aged 7 to 16 (CAD 11,000 for a child eligible for the disability tax credit), and two-thirds of the claimant’s earned income. In a couple, the spouse with the lower net income must claim it, except in a few listed situations. Because it is a deduction, it also lowers adjusted family net income, so the Canada child benefit for July 2026 to June 2027 rises by the CCB reduction rate times the deduction: 7%, 13.5%, 19% or 23% in the first band for one to four or more children, and 3.2% to 9.5% above CAD 82,847. In the default example, CAD 12,000 of care for two children comes back as about CAD 2,346 of tax and CAD 684 of CCB, about a quarter of the cost.

For a young child in a regulated full-time space, then, the amount paid is often what sets the deduction. The limits matter more for unregulated or private care, for nannies, and for school-age children whose before- and after-school care and summer day camps can exceed CAD 5,000. These are means of what parents reported, not the price of any particular space; your own receipts decide the claim.

National $435 a month is $5,220 a year, below the CAD 8,000 limit; where fees in regulated spaces have fallen under the federal–provincial early learning and child care agreements, expenses paid, not the CAD 8,000 limit, are more likely to set the deduction for a young child. Parents who pay for child care so they can work can deduct part of it on line 21400 of their return. Most of the attention goes to the tax saving. But because it is a deduction rather than a credit, it also lowers net income, and adjusted family net income is what sets the Canada child benefit. A 2025 deduction therefore pays twice: once as a lower 2025 tax bill, and again as higher CCB payments from July 2026 to June 2027.

So as long as the family stays within one band and still gets some CCB, each dollar of deduction adds the band’s rate to the benefit. In the default case, CAD 12,000 of deduction at CAD 100,000 of family income adds 5.7% × CAD 12,000 = CAD 684, about CAD 57 a month. For a family with two children and income in the first band the same deduction adds CAD 1,620. Below CAD 38,237 the full benefit is already paid and the deduction adds nothing to it. The age bands differ from the deduction’s: a child who was 6 at the end of 2025 counts towards the CAD 8,000 limit but receives the 6-to-17 CCB amount, which is why the calculator asks separately how many children are under 6.

Statistics Canada reported in October 2025 that parents of children aged 0 to 5 in full-time centre-based care (30 hours or more a week) paid a mean of CAD 435 a month in 2025, down from CAD 663 in 2022 (the 2022 figure excludes the territories, and the survey sources differ). Provincial means ranged from CAD 206 in Prince Edward Island to CAD 571 in British Columbia. Multiplied by 12, even British Columbia’s mean is about CAD 6,852 a year, below the CAD 8,000 limit for one child under 7.

The CCB falls by a fixed percentage of income over $38,237 and a smaller one over $82,847; with 2 children those rates are 13.5% and 5.7%. So the deduction is worth most in the first band and little below $38,237, where the full benefit is already paid. Your family income: $100,000, extra CCB $684.00.

The calculator works out the deduction from CRA’s three limits, applies an editable tax rate to estimate the tax saved, and recomputes the CCB with and without the deduction. Its default is a couple with one child under 6 and one aged 7 to 16, CAD 12,000 of care paid for 2025, and net incomes of CAD 30,000 and CAD 70,000.

The deduction follows the amount paid until it meets the lower of the two dashed lines, then stays flat. Here that ceiling is $13,000. Anything paid above it gives no deduction and cannot be carried forward to another year.

The per-child amounts are pooled: a family with one child under 7 and one aged 9 has a combined limit of CAD 13,000, and can use it even if most of the cost is for the younger child. Expenses above the limits are simply lost; CRA’s how-to-claim page says unclaimed expenses cannot be carried forward. Eligible expenses include daycare, nursery school, day camps and day sports schools, and boarding schools and overnight camps up to a weekly amount; the care must let a parent work, run a business, study or do research, and payments to the child’s other parent or to a relative under 18 do not count.

The rule has two consequences that surprise families. First, the claim usually goes to the spouse in the lower tax bracket, so the tax saving is smaller than if the higher earner could claim. Second, a lower earner with little earned income hits the two-thirds limit: CAD 15,000 of earnings supports at most CAD 10,000 of deduction, whatever was paid.

Why the lower-income spouse claims

With 1 child under 7 and 1 aged 7 to 16, $12,000 of 2025 child care and $30,000 of earned income for the lower-income spouse, the deduction is $12,000, set by the expenses paid. The lower-income spouse claims, as CRA requires. At the assumed 19.55% marginal rate it saves $2,346.00 of income tax. It also lowers adjusted family net income from $100,000 to $88,000, which raises the July 2026 to June 2027 Canada child benefit from $8,040.28 to $8,724.28, $684.00 more. Together $3,030.00 comes back, 25.3% of what was paid. The tax rate is an assumption; provincial child care credits (such as Ontario’s CARE credit), the Canada disability benefit, GST/HST credit and other income-tested amounts are not included.
